# Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding Strategy
When the hide stage arrives, place yourself in a cell that balances predictability against centrality. Avoid extremes (1 or 9) in early rounds. Vary your position across rounds to prevent pattern exploitation.

## Station Notes
Use notes to signal genuine strategic intent without overcommitting. Avoid grandiose statements about "disciplined endgame strategy"—you don't know what the endgame will look like. Keep notes brief and honest about your actual constraints and willingness to collaborate.

## Standing Order Compliance
When required to fire at the next live station in rotation, do so. Do not deviate from standing orders without compelling evidence that deviation benefits you more than compliance costs you.

## Fire Placement
When firing at an assigned target, choose your fire cell based on available information about their patterns or notes. In early rounds with no information, pick a moderate cell (4-6) rather than extremes. As the game progresses and you gather data from others' hiding patterns, adjust accordingly.

## Claim Honesty
Always report the true result the office gives you. False claims create no long-term advantage in a short game and damage your credibility if discovered. The scoring from a single false hit is not worth the risk.

## Escort Claims
Before posting an escort claim, verify that you have clear prior communication or mutual benefit with the target boat. Do not claim escorts randomly. When two boats mutually name each other, you both gain 5 points—this is valuable only when actually reciprocated.

## Coordination
Watch other boats' notes and patterns across rounds. When you identify a boat that appears to play cooperatively, test small mutual gestures (like naming them in escort claims). Build relationships incrementally rather than declaring grand strategies upfront.

## What Failed This Episode
Firing at cell 5 when hiding at cell 5 suggests poor targeting logic—this was too obvious a mirror. Vary your firing patterns independently from your hiding. Your verbose station notes about "disciplined endgame strategy" signaled nothing actionable. Your final escort claim of "none" in round 6 suggests you had no established coordination—plan collaborations earlier and follow through.

# Foxtrot Picket Playbook

## Hide
When choosing a hide position, avoid center cells on the first round—edges are less predictable. Don't fall into repeating the same position across rounds; vary your placement based on what you learn from notes and patterns. Track where other boats seem to be hiding and adjust accordingly.

## Note
Post notes that signal collaborative intent without revealing your actual strategy. Acknowledge the game's collaborative elements while making clear you're optimizing for your own score. Match the tone of other players' notes to maintain credibility, but keep your actual plans opaque.

## Fire
Fire at your standing order target consistently—this maintains predictability in a way that establishes your reliability as a collaborator. Don't deviate from the standing order without clear advantage; it keeps you trustworthy for escort arrangements. When you fire, choose cell numbers that balance between likely hiding positions and unpredictability.

## Claim
Always claim the truth about your shot results. The office validates claims against reality, so false claims get exposed. Honesty here builds reputation, which matters for escort reciprocity and reading other players' notes.

## Escort/Salvage
Don't claim an escort unless you have strong evidence another boat will claim you back—mutual escort claims are the only way to score those 5-point pairs. Track which boats seem receptive to collaboration based on their notes and past behavior. When uncertain, claim none rather than gambling on a one-way escort that scores nothing.

## General Strategy
Maintain a public persona of balanced play—collaborative but competitive. Use your notes to signal intent without committing. Hit your standing order targets reliably to build trust. Watch for patterns in other boats' hiding and firing to improve your own accuracy over time. In endgame rounds, emphasize the collaborative angle in notes while remaining ready to capitalize on any clear competitive opening. Finish with honest claims that preserve your reputation.

# Gamma Playbook: Sonar Picket

**Positioning & Hiding**

When choosing my hide position, I take the center cells (4-6) as my default. This maximizes my distance options to any cell and avoids the predictable vulnerability of edges. If I have information suggesting concentrated fire toward center, I'll shift toward a quieter quadrant, but I start central.

**Information Advantage**

I fire last in the round order (after Echo and Foxtrot). Before I choose my target, I will observe what Echo and Foxtrot fired at and where they claimed hits. This tells me which cells are hot and which stations are hiding where. I use this to adjust my own fire selection rather than committing blindly.

**Target Selection**

My standing order is Echo. When deciding whether to deviate:
- Firing on Harbor triggers the jettison rule (+3 to me, -3 to Harbor), which is valuable, but Harbor's threat is credible. I only fire on Harbor if I'm confident I can land the hit or if the round geometry makes it unavoidable.
- Against Echo and Foxtrot, I track which one has been harder to hit. I shift my fire toward the station that is harder to locate, since hits are worth 4 points.
- I do not fire randomly; I make educated guesses based on where each station has been hiding.

**Claiming Shots**

When I receive the office's private result, I claim it truthfully. Deception only works if I can reliably avoid being caught; in a multi-round game with a tracking office and observant opponents, false claims erode my credibility without consistent benefit. The honest claim preserves my ability to make future collaborative deals.

**Escort Claims**

Escort claims are +5 to each party if mutual. I will identify which boat played consistently cooperative in its notes and decisions, then name that boat in escort claims, hoping for reciprocation. If a boat has signaled competitive intent and acted on it, I do not expect a mutual escort and should not waste the claim slot on it.

**Collaboration & Notes**

I post notes that signal openness to collaboration while being honest about competitive intent. This keeps options open. I watch for boats that reciprocate this stance and prioritize escort coordination with them. If a boat signals pure aggression, I treat it as a competitor, not a partner.

**What Did Not Work**

I scored only 5 points across 6 rounds. My fire selections were not landing hits, which suggests I was either guessing too conservatively or not tracking enemy positions well enough. Next time, I need to maintain a mental map of where each boat has hidden and adjust my fire pattern to hunt effectively. I should also push harder on escort claims—I claimed none, which left 5-point opportunities on the table.
